story: Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme in your blood that pulls CO2 out of tissue - without it you could not exhale. It is also the example ESM3's developers use to show off the model. The old catalytic core is fixed; your job is the flanks that wrap around it. Engineers are now using the same enzyme chemistry to build carbon-capture systems for CO2 removal.
intensity_why: Most of the protein is fixed; the model only designs the flanks, and the fixed core keeps it on track.
expected: A soluble mixed alpha/beta fold around the fixed core. pLDDT is usually high in the core and more variable in the designed flanks.

story: Renal dipeptidase (PDB 1ITU) is the human enzyme that shreds carbapenem antibiotics in the kidney - it is why the drug imipenem has to be given together with an inhibitor of this exact enzyme. Its helix-coil motif (residues ~124-147) does the chemistry. Keep that motif exactly as it is, in sequence and in 3D, and have ESM3 invent a brand-new protein around it - one more way to hold the motif in place, and a template for anyone designing an inhibitor.
intensity_why: The motif is fixed in sequence AND 3D structure, but the scaffold around it is fully invented.
expected: A novel fold holding the motif; motif pLDDT high (it is fixed), scaffold pLDDT varies with length.

story: No motif, no template, no evolutionary history - just 100 blank positions. In 2003 the Baker lab needed years of computation to design Top7, the first protein with a truly new fold. ESM3 attempts the same thing in minutes. When you present, be ready for the hardest question of the day: how much can you trust a confidence score on something evolution never made?
intensity_why: Nothing is fixed, so every confidence number is an educated guess outside the model's comfort zone.
expected: A compact mostly-alpha or alpha/beta fold. Expect the widest confidence spread in the class - and the best share-out story.

story: Cone snails harpoon fish with venom peptides held together by disulfide bonds - and one of them, ziconotide, is an approved painkiller stronger than morphine. Keep the cysteine pattern that makes these peptides small and stable, and let ESM3 fill in everything between. The catch: the cysteines have to pair up correctly in 3D, or the design falls apart.
intensity_why: Short protein, but the disulfide-pairing constraint is unforgiving - check the pairs in 3D.
expected: Small cysteine-rich structure; check whether the Cys residues end up paired in 3D (they often do not - good discussion).

story: About a quarter of all drugs work on membrane proteins - receptors and channels embedded in the cell surface - yet they remain among the hardest proteins to design and study. You plant hydrophobic bands (L/I/V) where the cell membrane would sit and let ESM3 connect them into a bundle. In a real membrane protein the water-hating residues all point outward into the oily core of the membrane. After you generate, check whether your design does the same - if they are scattered, the protein would never survive in a membrane.
intensity_why: Membrane proteins are rare in the training data, so the model has fewer examples to lean on.
expected: Alpha-helical bundle; the hydrophobic residues should all face the same direction, ready to sink into a membrane. Worth discussing: how would ESM3 know anything about membranes?

problem: A peptide that switches on in tumors
story: Tumors are more acidic than healthy tissue (about pH 6.5 vs 7.4), and drug designers use that difference: histidine changes charge right around pH 6.5, so histidine-rich peptides can unfold on arrival at a tumor. Fix histidines at regular intervals as the pH sensor and let ESM3 design the rest. You also run at the highest temperature on the menu, so expect big differences between candidates - that is the point.
intensity_why: Highest temperature on the menu: lots of variety between candidates, and little way to predict what you will get.
expected: Helical peptide with histidines lined up along one edge; expect the most diversity between candidates.

problem: Nature's LEGO: a programmable drug carrier
story: Repeat proteins - ankyrins, DARPins, TAL effectors - are biology's LEGO bricks: near-identical modules stacked into rigid scaffolds that carry drug payloads or grip disease proteins, and several designed-repeat drugs are in clinical trials. You fix a periodic leucine anchor every 7 residues - exactly one helical turn - and see whether ESM3 builds the ladder.
intensity_why: The periodic pattern is a strong hint, but long repetitive designs test the model's limits.
expected: A long, stretched-out spiral rather than a compact ball - the most unusual shape any team will see.

problem: Repair p53, the guardian of the genome
story: p53 stops cells with damaged DNA from dividing - and it is mutated in about half of all human cancers. Some mutations kill p53 by wrecking its fold: the Y220C mutation opens a crack in the core and the protein falls apart at body temperature, which is why drug companies are hunting for molecules that glue the crack shut. Your job is the protein-designer version of that: fold a fragment of the mutant protein, read where the model loses confidence, then run the design cycle - inverse-fold a repaired sequence for the same shape, refold, and see whether your repair scores better.
intensity_why: Iterative workflow (fold -> inverse-fold -> refold); the verdict depends on comparing two confidence reports.
expected: The round-tripped candidate should score higher mean pLDDT than the mutant starting point. If it does not, that is also worth presenting - discuss why.

story: A jellyfish protein lit up biology: green fluorescent protein won the 2008 Nobel Prize, and engineers have been redesigning it ever since - it is why labs today glow in blue, green, red, and far-red. You fix almost the whole protein, including the three residues that make the light, and let ESM3 redesign one 24-residue stretch. The question: does the barrel survive, and would it still glow?
intensity_why: Only 24 of 238 residues are the model's to design; the fixed barrel keeps everything anchored.
expected: The beta-barrel should survive with the redesigned stretch; pLDDT high across the fixed regions, more variable in the redesigned stretch. If the barrel breaks, that is the share-out story.

story: In 2016 scientists found a bacterium at a Japanese recycling plant that eats plastic: Ideonella sakaiensis, armed with PETase, an enzyme that cuts PET bottles into their building blocks. Real labs have since engineered faster, heat-tolerant versions - and the recipe is always the same: keep the chemistry, redesign the scaffold. You fix the catalytic machinery and let ESM3 redesign one stretch. Could your variant be the next plastic-eating enzyme?
intensity_why: The catalytic machinery is fixed; the model only redesigns one stretch away from the active site.
expected: The fold and the catalytic motif should survive; the redesigned stretch is the question mark. Compare with team 9: same recipe, different protein.
